procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention under s. 3(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not applicable. The case originated as a writ petition directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a petition under Art. 32 of the Constitution challenging his detention on the ground that the State Government did not consider his representation of June 23, 1969 with reasonable and proper expedition. The Supreme Court allowed the petition and set the petitioner at liberty.

directions: The petitioner is set at liberty.
The petitioner is ordered to be released forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether the State Government failed to consider the petitioner's representation against his detention with reasonable and proper expedition, thereby violating his constitutional rights.

facts: The petitioner was detained on June 7, 1969, and submitted a representation against his detention to the State Government on June 23, 1969.
The State Government placed the case, including the representation, before the Advisory Board on July 1, 1969.
The Advisory Board gave its opinion on August 13, 1969.
The State Government finally rejected the petitioner's representation on August 19, 1969, nearly two months after it was submitted.

The State Government claimed the delay was due to making its own inquiries through the Superintendent of Railway Police, but provided no specific details about when this inquiry was ordered, how long it took, or why it was delayed.
The Superintendent who allegedly conducted the inquiry did not file an affidavit to explain the delay.
law: The Supreme Court established that the appropriate government has a constitutional obligation to consider a detenu's representation as early and expeditiously as possible.
This duty is independent of the proceedings of the Advisory Board. The government cannot delay its own consideration of the representation while waiting for the Advisory Board's opinion.
The reason for this urgency is that the fundamental right and personal liberty of a citizen are at stake, and any delay is an unconstitutional and irresponsible act.
application: The Court found that the delay of nearly two months between the petitioner's representation (June 23) and the government's rejection (August 19) was "inordinate."

The State's explanation for the delay was deemed insufficient and unacceptable. The Court noted the lack of an affidavit from the officer who actually conducted the inquiry and the absence of any information explaining the timeline or reasons for the long delay.

The Court concluded that the State Government was guilty of two constitutional infractions: first, the inordinate and unexplained delay, and second, improperly "putting off the consideration till after the receipt of the opinion of the Advisory Board."
This demonstrated "inactivity and lack of independent judgment" on the part of the government, which amounted to a failure to discharge its constitutional duty.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the State Government failed to discharge its constitutional obligation to consider the petitioner's representation with proper and reasonable expedition. This failure violated the petitioner's rights, and therefore, the Court allowed the petition and ordered the petitioner to be set at liberty.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the State Government failed to consider the petitioner's representation against his detention with reasonable and proper expedition, thereby violating his constitutional rights.
appellant_arguments: The government did not consider the petitioner's representation, made on June 23, 1969, with reasonable and proper expedition.
The government improperly delayed consideration of the representation until after it had received the opinion of the Advisory Board.
There was an inordinate and unexplained delay in considering the representation, which constitutes a failure by the appropriate authority to discharge its constitutional obligation.
respondent_arguments: The government discharged its duty by referring the matter and the petitioner's representation to the Advisory Board.
The government considered and rejected the representation on August 19, 1969, after receiving the Advisory Board's report.
The delay was due to the time it took to conduct further inquiries into the representation through the Superintendent of Railway Police.

cases.case_name: Sk. Abdul Karim & Ors. v. The State of West Bengal
cases.principle: The appropriate Government cannot be said to discharge its obligation merely by forwarding the representation of the detenu to the Advisory Board; Article 22 of the Constitution guarantees the right of a detenu to have a proper consideration of the representation by the appropriate authority itself.

cases.case_name: Pankaj Kumar Chakrabarty & Ors. v. The State of West Bengal
cases.principle: The obligation of the appropriate authority to consider the detenu's representation under section 7 of the Act is entirely independent of any action by the Advisory Board. The representation is addressed to the Government so that it can exercise its own opinion and judgment in an independent and honest manner.

cases.case_name: Khairul Haque v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: It was applied to support the conclusion that the appropriate authority failed to discharge its constitutional obligation by inactivity and lack of independent judgment in considering the detenu's representation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The appropriate government has a constitutional obligation to consider a detenu's representation as expeditiously as possible. Any inordinate delay in this consideration, or postponing it until after receiving the opinion of the Advisory Board, violates the detenu's fundamental right.
obiter: Even if the Advisory Board expresses an opinion against the release of a detenu, the government may still exercise its power to release the detenu.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The State of West Bengal was guilty of infraction of the constitutional provisions not only by inordinate delay of the consideration of the representation but also by putting off the consideration till after the receipt of the opinion of the Advisory Board. There was no explanation for this inordinate delay. The State had given no information as to why this long delay occurred. The inescapable conclusion in the present case is that the appropriate authority failed to discharge its constitutional obligation by inactivity and lack of independent judgment.
legal_tests_applied: The appropriate authority is bound to consider the representation of the detenu as early as possible.
The appropriate Government is to exercise its opinion and judgment on the representation before sending the case along with the detenu's representation to the Advisory Board.
The appropriate authority is to consider the representation of the detenu uninfluenced by any opinion or consideration of the Advisory Board.
policy_considerations: The personal liberty of a person is at stake. Any delay would not only be an irresponsible act on the part of the appropriate authority but also unconstitutional because the Constitution enshrines the fundamental right of a detenu to have his representation considered and it is imperative that when the liberty of a person is in peril immediate action should be taken by the relevant authorities.
A citizen's right raises a correlative duty of the State.
